extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, especially fantasy authors designing magic systems
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to design and use magic systems in fantasy fiction, including a core principle relating explainability to narrative utility and concrete advice for soft, hard, and hybrid systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanderson's First Law (core principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: An author’s ability to solve conflict with magic is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to how well the reader understands said magic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central rule: the more the reader understands what the magic can do, the more legitimate and satisfying it is for the author to use that magic to resolve conflicts. If the reader doesn't understand the magic, using it to solve problems risks deus ex machina and undermines the plot. Use this as the baseline when deciding how and when magic can resolve story problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft Magic (use for wonder, not plot solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic with few explicit rules, meant to establish a sense of wonder and the sense that characters are small compared to vast forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soft magic should rarely be used to solve problems; instead use it for visuals, ambiance, and to create problems. If characters try to use the magic, it should not reliably do what they expect. Examples: Tolkien (mystical, vague magic); George R. R. Martin (magic creates problems or complications). Anti-pattern: allowing soft magic to be the solution to key plot points, which removes tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hard Magic (explicit rules, magic as a tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic systems where the author explicitly describes rules and capabilities so the reader understands what the magic can do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With hard magic you can legitimately have characters use magic to solve problems because the reader understands its limits and possibilities. Hard magic supports clever problem-solving, twists, and worldbuilding. Examples: Asimov's robot laws, superhero power sets. Important: outline rules and avoid violating them casually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle Ground / Hybrid Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixture where individual books may have specific, consistent rules (hard) while the larger setting remains somewhat vague (soft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can combine approaches—e.g., J.K. Rowling: specific rules in a given book but an expanding, sometimes inconsistent system across a series. This allows use of magic in climaxes while preserving overall wonder. Be mindful of contradictions and 'forgetting' abilities; minor lapses may be acceptable if they don't harm the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide the desired feel/mood before designing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether you want techno-magic (hard), hybrids, or vague/mystical magic (soft) based on the mood and narrative needs of your book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what is most interesting to you and what best matches the book's tone. Different feels suit different audiences and stories; experiment and pick what you enjoy and can sustain. Sanderson notes his own preference for rules, costs, and laws because they make writing more fun for him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist using magic to solve problems unless already explained
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give heroes a new power or introduce a rule solely when you need it to resolve a particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid writing laws into the system just to use them in a single case—this makes magic seem flimsy and convenient. If you need a capability shown in the climax, it should be established earlier or be a credible extension of existing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using hard magic, force characters to use existing knowledge/resources
rubrics_metrics.description: When characters encounter problems, they should use what they already have and know rather than being given new powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: 'How could the characters use what they already have and know to solve this conflict?' Making characters stretch to apply their known abilities increases interest, character development, and reader satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using soft magic, prefer non-magic solutions or complications
rubrics_metrics.description: In soft-magic stories, conflicts should be resolved without relying on magic, or magic should complicate the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: 'How can they solve this without magic?' or 'How can using the magic to TRY to solve the problem really just make things worse?' Using magic to backfire or create further consequences preserves tension and wonder (example: Gandalf and the Balrog incident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make magic facilitate narrative and provide a source of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Magic should enhance mood, be visually appealing, and serve narrative purposes rather than merely being ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design magic so it both fits the setting visually and actively contributes to plot and character dilemmas. If it neither affects plot nor mood, it is wasted worldbuilding; if it resolves plot without justification, it undermines the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance explanation and mystery to allow revelations later
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain the magic as simply as possible while leaving background and exceptions for later discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can design a complicated system but reveal it gradually—this preserves mystery and enables later plot revelations. Sanderson describes having many background rules that aren't fully explained at first, allowing discoveries across books. Be careful to plant groundwork so later revelations feel earned.
